questions.question: A page has two <script defer> tags and one <script async> tag, each pointing to a different file. Which statement about their execution order is accurate?
options: The async script always runs first because it downloads in parallel with parsing.
All three scripts execute in the exact order they appear in the HTML, regardless of the async attribute.
The async script waits until both defer scripts have finished before running.
The two defer scripts run in the order they appear in the document; the async script may run before, between, or after them.
hints: Think about what defer guarantees that async does not.
defer preserves document order and runs after parsing; async has no ordering guarantee relative to other scripts.
questions.explanation: Scripts with defer execute in the order they appear in the document, after HTML parsing completes and before DOMContentLoaded. Scripts with async run as soon as they've downloaded, with no guaranteed order relative to other scripts.

questions.question: You open a <dialog> with showModal(), and none of its descendants have the autofocus attribute. Where does keyboard focus go?
options: Focus stays on whatever element had focus before the dialog opened.
Focus moves to the first focusable element nested inside the dialog.
Focus moves to the <body> element.
Focus moves to the dialog's close button, which is created automatically.
hints: showModal() always moves focus somewhere inside the dialog by default.
Without an explicit autofocus target, the browser picks a default based on the dialog's contents.
questions.explanation: When showModal() opens a <dialog> without an autofocus descendant, focus is placed on the first nested focusable element inside the dialog. Adding autofocus lets you override this default.

questions.question: Which containers does the CSS gap shorthand actually apply to?
options: Multi-column, flex, and grid containers
Grid containers only
Flex and block containers, but not grid
Only elements with display: flow-root
hints: gap isn't limited to just one layout mode.
It works anywhere you have rows/columns to space out: multicol, flexbox, and grid.
questions.explanation: The gap shorthand sets row and column gaps in multi-column, flex, and grid containers. A common misconception is that it only works with CSS Grid, but it applies to flex containers too.

questions.question: You set z-index: 10 on a <div> that has no position property set (so it stays position: static) and is not a flex or grid item. What happens?
options: The div is stacked above all its unpositioned siblings.
The browser throws a console warning and ignores the whole rule block.
The div creates a new stacking context but keeps its default paint order.
The z-index value has no effect, because it only applies to positioned elements or flex/grid items.
hints: z-index has a prerequisite before it does anything.
It only kicks in for elements that are positioned, or that are flex/grid items.
questions.explanation: z-index sets the stacking order of a positioned element (or a flex/grid item) and its descendants. On a statically positioned, non-flex/grid-item element, z-index is simply ignored.

questions.question: You call structuredClone() on an object that contains a function property. What happens?
options: The function is silently dropped from the clone.
structuredClone() throws a DataCloneError.
The function is copied by reference into the clone.
The function is serialized to its source code string.
hints: Not every JavaScript value is 'structured-clonable'.
Values that can't be serialized by the structured clone algorithm cause an exception rather than being silently skipped.
questions.explanation: structuredClone() throws a DataCloneError DOMException when asked to clone a value that isn't serializable. Function objects (and DOM nodes) cannot be duplicated by the structured clone algorithm.

questions.question: In the expression a?.b.c.d, if a is null, what happens to the rest of the chain (.c.d)?
options: JavaScript still evaluates .c.d and throws because b is undefined.
A SyntaxError is thrown because chaining after ?. requires another ?. at each step.
The entire expression short-circuits and evaluates to undefined without evaluating .c or .d.
Only .b is skipped; .c.d is evaluated against undefined and returns null.
hints: Optional chaining doesn't just protect the one property access right after it.
Once the short-circuit condition is hit, the whole rest of the chain is skipped, not just the next property.
questions.explanation: If the value before ?. is null or undefined, the entire chained expression short-circuits and evaluates to undefined immediately. None of the remaining property accesses are evaluated, and no error is thrown.

questions.question: Relative to the actual moment a target element's visibility crosses a threshold, when does an IntersectionObserver callback run?
options: Asynchronously, on the main thread, some time after the intersection change.
Synchronously, in the same task that caused the layout change.
On a separate worker thread, so it never blocks the main thread.
Only once, the first time observe() is called, regardless of later changes.
hints: This is part of why IntersectionObserver is considered cheaper than scroll-event polling.
The callback isn't invoked in the same synchronous flow as the layout/scroll change; the API is inherently asynchronous.
questions.explanation: The Intersection Observer API asynchronously observes changes in the intersection of a target element with an ancestor element or the viewport, so callbacks fire on the main thread but not synchronously with the layout change itself.

questions.question: You write new FormData(myFormElement), where myFormElement is a reference to an existing <form>. What ends up in the FormData object?
options: Nothing — FormData must be built manually with append() calls.
Only the form's text <input> values; file inputs are skipped.
Only fields that have a name and are currently focused.
The form's current field values, including file input contents.
hints: The FormData constructor accepts a form element as an optional argument.
When given a <form>, it captures the submittable fields' current values as they'd be sent on submission — that includes files.
questions.explanation: Passing a <form> element to the FormData() constructor captures the current values of the form's fields, including file input content, exactly as they'd be encoded for a multipart/form-data submission.

questions.question: An element has both an aria-label attribute and an aria-labelledby attribute pointing to visible text elsewhere on the page. Which one determines the accessible name?
options: aria-label always wins because it's simpler and more direct.
Whichever attribute was added to the DOM more recently wins.
aria-labelledby takes precedence over aria-label and even the element's own visible text.
Assistive technologies concatenate both into a single accessible name.
hints: The two attributes aren't equal in priority when both are present.
One of them is documented as having the highest precedence in accessible name computation, overriding the other and even the element's contents.
questions.explanation: aria-labelledby has the highest precedence when browsers calculate the accessible name. If both attributes are present, aria-labelledby is used, overriding aria-label and even the element's own visible text.

questions.question: A user clicks a button with their mouse, and a different user tabs to the same button with the keyboard. Why might the button show a focus ring only for the keyboard user?
options: It's a bug — :focus applies identically regardless of input method.
Browsers apply :focus-visible based on a heuristic that decides whether a focus indicator should be shown, typically favoring keyboard interaction over mouse clicks.
Focus rings are controlled entirely by the tabindex value, not the input device.
:focus-visible only exists in browser DevTools and has no effect on real users.
hints: There's a CSS pseudo-class specifically designed to distinguish 'focus that should be visibly indicated' from focus in general.
:focus-visible matches when the user agent's heuristic determines a focus indicator should be shown — this commonly differs for keyboard vs. pointer interaction.
questions.explanation: :focus-visible applies while an element matches :focus and the user agent determines, via heuristics, that a focus indicator should be shown, commonly leading browsers to show a focus ring for keyboard interaction but not for mouse clicks.

questions.question: Inside a block, you read a let variable on the line before its declaration. What happens?
options: A ReferenceError is thrown
It evaluates to undefined
It evaluates to null
The declaration is hoisted with its value
hints: let variables sit in the temporal dead zone until their declaration runs.
var behaves differently — it would give undefined.
questions.explanation: From the start of the block until execution reaches the declaration, a let variable is in the temporal dead zone; any access throws a ReferenceError. This differs from var, which yields undefined when accessed before its declaration.

questions.question: One of the five promises passed to Promise.all() rejects. What does the returned promise do?
options: Rejects immediately with that first rejection reason
Waits for all five to settle, then rejects with an array of errors
Fulfills with the four successful values
Fulfills with null in the rejected promise's position
hints: Promise.all is fail-fast.
A different combinator, Promise.allSettled, waits for every outcome.
questions.explanation: Promise.all rejects when any of the input promises rejects, with that first rejection reason — it does not wait for the others. It fulfills only when all inputs fulfill, with an array of their values in order.

questions.question: What does [5, 12, 8].at(-1) return?
options: undefined
An error — negative indexes are invalid
hints: at() accepts negative integers.
They count back from the last item.
questions.explanation: Array.prototype.at() accepts negative integers, which count back from the last item — so at(-1) returns the final element, 8. Truly out-of-range indexes return undefined instead of throwing.

questions.question: How much specificity does the :where() pseudo-class contribute to a selector?
options: Always zero
The specificity of its most specific argument
One class-level of specificity
The same as an id selector
hints: :is() behaves differently from :where() here.
This difference is why :where() is popular in CSS resets.
questions.explanation: :where() always has zero specificity, whereas :is() takes on the specificity of its most specific argument. That makes :where() ideal for base styles that later rules should override easily.

questions.question: An element with position: sticky scrolls normally and never sticks. What is the most likely cause?
options: No inset property (like top) is set to a non-auto value
The element is missing a z-index
Its parent is missing overflow: hidden
Sticky only works on table elements
hints: Sticky needs a threshold that tells it where to stick.
Without one, MDN says sticky behaves like another position value.
questions.explanation: At least one inset property (top, right, bottom, left, or a logical equivalent) must be non-auto on the sticky axis. If both inset properties for an axis are auto, sticky behaves as relative on that axis — the classic cause of a sticky element that never sticks.

questions.question: A fetch() was given an AbortSignal, and the controller's abort() is called mid-request. How does the fetch promise settle?
options: It rejects with a DOMException named AbortError
It resolves with response.ok set to false
It resolves with undefined
It stays pending forever
hints: Aborting is an error path, not a success path.
The rejection carries a specifically-named DOMException.
questions.explanation: When abort() is called, the fetch() promise rejects with a DOMException named AbortError — code handling aborts should catch it and distinguish it from network failures.

questions.question: Which storage survives a page reload but is cleared when its tab closes, and is not shared with other tabs?
options: sessionStorage
localStorage
IndexedDB
Cookies without an expiry
hints: A page session lasts as long as the tab is open.
The storage in question is partitioned by origin and tab.
questions.explanation: sessionStorage data lasts for the page session: it survives reloads and restores, but closing the tab ends the session and clears it, and it is partitioned per tab — unlike localStorage, which persists and is shared across all same-origin tabs.

questions.question: A <button> element inside a <form> has no type attribute. What happens when it is clicked?
options: It submits the form data
It does nothing until a type is set
It resets the form to its initial values
It only fires its click handler, never affecting the form
hints: The default depends on whether the button is associated with a form.
MDN's notes warn to set type="button" on buttons that shouldn't submit.
questions.explanation: For buttons associated with a form, type defaults to submit when the attribute is missing, empty, or invalid — so clicking submits the form. Give non-submitting buttons an explicit type="button" to avoid accidental submissions.

questions.question: What happens to the markup nested inside a <template> element when the page loads?
options: It is not rendered; it is held in a DocumentFragment exposed by the template's content property
It renders immediately like any other markup
It renders but is hidden with display: none
It is moved to the end of <body> automatically
hints: The element's content is deliberately not shown by default.
A read-only property on HTMLTemplateElement exposes the subtree.
questions.explanation: A template's content is not rendered by default, and the nested markup does not become regular children of the element — it lives in a DocumentFragment exposed by the read-only content property, ready to be cloned into the document with JavaScript.

questions.question: What does aria-hidden="true" actually change about an element?
options: It removes the element and its children from the accessibility tree; visual rendering is unchanged
It visually hides the element like display: none
It hides it both visually and from assistive technology
Nothing, unless CSS also hides it
hints: Screen reader users and sighted users end up with different experiences.
MDN warns against putting it on focusable elements.
questions.explanation: aria-hidden="true" hides content from assistive technology by removing the element and all its children from the accessibility tree, while changing nothing visually. It should not be used on focusable elements — and because children inherit, it should not be added to the parent or ancestor of a focusable element.

questions.question: What does typeof null evaluate to, and why?
options: "object", due to a bug preserved from the first JavaScript implementation
"null", matching its primitive type
"undefined", because null has no type
"object" only in non-strict mode
hints: The answer surprises almost everyone the first time.
It traces back to how values were tagged in the original engine.
questions.explanation: In the first JavaScript implementation, values used a type tag plus a value. Objects used type tag 0, and null was stored as the NULL pointer (0x00), which also carried tag 0. As a result, typeof null has always returned "object". A fix making typeof null === "null" was proposed for ECMAScript and rejected.

questions.question: const qty = 0; console.log(qty ?? 42, qty || 42); — what is logged?
hints: ?? only falls back for null and undefined.
|| falls back for any falsy value, and 0 is falsy.
questions.explanation: The nullish coalescing operator returns its right-hand side only when the left is null or undefined, so 0 ?? 42 preserves the 0. Logical OR returns the right side for any falsy left operand, so 0 || 42 yields 42.

questions.question: When does a callback scheduled with queueMicrotask() run?
options: After the current task completes, before control returns to the event loop
Immediately, interrupting the current code
On the next animation frame
After all pending timers have fired
hints: Microtasks drain before the browser regains control.
That is earlier than any timer callback can run.
questions.explanation: Microtasks are executed after the current task completes, but before control is returned to the browser's event loop — so they run ahead of the next task, like a timer callback. Libraries and frameworks use them to batch work before the browser moves on.

questions.question: When does the aspect-ratio property actually affect an element's dimensions?
options: When at least one of the element's sizes is automatic
Always, overriding width and height
Only on replaced elements like images
Only when both width and height are set explicitly
hints: The ratio participates in the calculation of auto sizes.
With both dimensions fixed, there is nothing left for the ratio to decide.
questions.explanation: aspect-ratio defines a preferred width-to-height ratio used when calculating auto sizes. At least one of the box's sizes must be automatic — if neither width nor height is automatic, the provided ratio has no effect on the box's preferred sizes.

questions.question: In a default horizontal, left-to-right document, which physical properties does margin-inline set?
options: margin-left and margin-right
margin-top and margin-bottom
All four margins
No physical margins — it is purely virtual
hints: Inline is the axis text flows along.
The mapping depends on writing-mode, direction, and text-orientation.
questions.explanation: margin-inline is a logical shorthand for the inline start and end margins. Its physical mapping depends on writing-mode, direction, and text-orientation; in a default horizontal LTR document it corresponds to margin-left and margin-right.

questions.question: Which baseline condition must be met before the async Clipboard API is available at all?
options: A secure context (HTTPS)
A registered service worker
A user gesture within the last 10 minutes
The page must be installed as a PWA
hints: The API is gated the same way service workers are.
Reading additionally requires recent user interaction.
questions.explanation: The Clipboard API reads and writes the system clipboard only in secure contexts (HTTPS). On top of that, reading expects recent user interaction (transient activation) and writing may require the clipboard-write permission.

questions.question: fetch() receives a 404 response from the server. What happens to the promise?
options: It resolves normally, and response.ok is false
It rejects with a NotFound error
It resolves with an empty body and ok true
It retries once, then rejects
hints: fetch only rejects on network-level failures.
ok reflects a specific status range.
questions.explanation: A 404 does not reject fetch — the promise resolves, and response.ok is false because ok is true only for statuses in the 200–299 range. Code must check response.ok (or status) itself to treat HTTP errors as failures.

questions.question: You write <details open="false">…</details>. How does the browser render it?
options: Expanded — the details are visible
Collapsed, because the value is false
It is treated as invalid markup and ignored
Collapsed on first load, expanded after interaction
hints: open is a Boolean attribute.
For Boolean attributes, presence matters — not the value.
questions.explanation: open is a Boolean attribute: the details are shown whenever the attribute exists, regardless of its value, so open="false" still shows them. To hide the details you must remove the attribute entirely.

questions.question: What does loading="lazy" on an element do?
options: Defers loading the image until it reaches a browser-calculated distance from the viewport
Loads a low-quality placeholder first, then the full image
Loads the image only after every other resource has finished
Blocks rendering until the image enters the viewport
hints: The default value, eager, loads the image immediately.
The browser decides the distance threshold, not the author.
questions.explanation: loading="lazy" defers fetching until the image reaches a distance from the viewport calculated by the browser, avoiding network and storage cost for images that may never be needed. The default, eager, loads immediately regardless of viewport position.

questions.question: What does alt="" (an empty alt attribute) on an convey?
options: The image is not a key part of the content, and non-visual browsers may omit it
The alt text is missing and should be flagged as an error
Screen readers should announce the file name instead
The image failed to load
hints: An empty alt is a deliberate statement, not an omission.
Visual browsers also hide the broken-image icon for it.
questions.explanation: alt="" declares the image is not a key part of the content — decoration or a tracking pixel — so non-visual browsers may omit it from rendering. That is different from a missing alt attribute, which leaves assistive technology with nothing useful.

questions.question: Which values can be used as keys in a Map?
options: Any value, including objects and functions
Only strings
Only strings and symbols
Only primitives
hints: This is a key difference from plain objects.
Object keys are limited to two types.
questions.explanation: Both objects and primitive values may be used as Map keys (or values). Plain Object keys must be a String or a Symbol; anything else is coerced to a string.

questions.question: What does [1, [2, [3]]].flat() return when called with no arguments?
options: [1, [2, [3]]] unchanged
hints: flat takes a depth parameter.
Its default is not Infinity.
questions.explanation: flat()'s depth parameter defaults to 1, so only one level of nesting is flattened: [1, 2, [3]]. Pass a larger depth — or Infinity — to flatten deeper structures.

questions.question: const user = { name: "Ara" }; user.name = "Owl"; — what happens?
options: The property updates; const only prevents reassigning the binding
A TypeError, because const values are immutable
A silent failure — the property keeps its old value
It works only in non-strict mode
hints: const creates an immutable binding, not an immutable value.
Reassigning user itself is what would throw.
questions.explanation: const creates an immutable reference: the identifier cannot be reassigned, but the value it holds is not immutable. An object's properties can still be added, updated, or removed. Only reassigning user itself would throw.

questions.question: In a grid template, what does minmax(200px, 1fr) define for a track?
options: A size range: at least 200px and at most 1fr
Exactly 200px unless the grid overflows
A track that is always 1fr with 200px of padding
The minimum gap between two tracks
hints: The function name describes exactly what it clamps.
It is used with CSS grids.
questions.explanation: minmax() defines a size range greater than or equal to its minimum and less than or equal to its maximum. So, the track stays at least 200px and can expand to one fraction of the remaining free space.

questions.question: What does the currentColor keyword resolve to?
options: The value of the element's own color property
The nearest ancestor's background-color
The browser's default accent color
Always black unless overridden
hints: It lets borders and backgrounds follow the text color.
On the color property itself, it takes the inherited value.
questions.explanation: currentColor represents the value of the element's color property, letting other properties (like border or background) follow the text color. Used on the color property itself, it resolves to the inherited color value. Inside an SVG it makes the graphic inherit its parent's color — commonly used for icons nested inside a link.

questions.question: What does the prefers-reduced-motion: reduce media feature detect?
options: A device setting where the user asked to minimize non-essential motion
Automatic detection of a slow GPU
The device being in low-power mode
A viewport too small for animations
hints: It reflects an explicit user preference, not device performance.
Respecting it matters for people with vestibular motion disorders.
questions.explanation: prefers-reduced-motion detects whether the user has enabled a device setting to minimize non-essential motion — conveying that they prefer an interface that removes, reduces, or replaces motion-based animations. reduce evaluates as true; no-preference as false.

questions.question: params.get("missing") is called on a URLSearchParams with no such parameter. What is returned?
options: null
undefined
An empty string
It throws a RangeError
hints: get() returns the first value when the parameter exists.
The absent case mirrors Map-like APIs, not plain objects.
questions.explanation: URLSearchParams.get() returns the first value associated with the parameter, or null if the parameter is not found — not undefined or an empty string.

questions.question: A page writes to localStorage. Where does the resulting storage event fire?
options: In other same-origin browsing contexts — not in the window that made the change
In the window that made the change
In every open tab regardless of origin
Nowhere unless explicitly dispatched
hints: The event exists so other contexts can react to changes.
The initiating window already knows what it did.
questions.explanation: The Window storage event fires when another document that shares the same storage area (localStorage or sessionStorage) with the current window updates that storage. It does not fire in the window that performed the update. Unlike localStorage, whose storage event fires in all other same-origin tabs, the sessionStorage storage event fires only in browsing contexts within the current tab.

questions.question: How do you connect an <input> to a <datalist> of suggestions?
options: Set the input's list attribute to the datalist's id
Nest the input inside the datalist element
Add a for attribute on the datalist pointing at the input
Give both elements the same name attribute
hints: The datalist needs a unique identifier.
An attribute on the input references that identifier.
questions.explanation: Give the datalist a unique id and set the input's list attribute to the same value. The datalist provides suggestions only. The input can still accept any value that passes validation, unlike a <select>.

questions.question: When should a live region use aria-live="assertive" instead of "polite"?
options: Only when the interruption is imperative — time-critical information
Whenever you want users to notice the update
For all form validation messages
Never — assertive is deprecated
hints: Assertive updates interrupt immediately and can clear the speech queue.
MDN's warning: interruptions may disorient users.
questions.explanation: assertive gives updates the highest priority and presents them immediately, potentially clearing the queue of previous updates. Because an interruption may disorient users or stop them completing their task, MDN warns not to use assertive unless the interruption is imperative.

questions.question: Why is Array.isArray(value) preferred over value instanceof Array?
options: instanceof fails for arrays created in another realm, like an iframe
instanceof also matches array-like objects
Array.isArray is shorter to type, nothing more
instanceof throws for null values
hints: Each realm has its own Array constructor identity.
typeof is no help either — it reports "object" for arrays.
questions.explanation: Array.isArray() rejects values that aren't true Array instances, even if their prototype chain includes Array.prototype, and it accepts arrays created in other realms (like iframes or workers). By contrast, instanceof Array returns true in the first case and false in the second, leading to both false positives and false negatives.

questions.question: JSON.stringify({ a: undefined, b: [undefined] }) — what is produced?
options: {"b":[null]}
{"a":null,"b":[null]}
{"a":undefined,"b":[undefined]}
A TypeError is thrown
hints: undefined is not a valid JSON value.
The treatment differs between object properties and array elements.
questions.explanation: undefined, functions, and symbols are not valid JSON values: as object property values they are omitted entirely, while inside arrays they are changed to null — so the a property disappears and the array element becomes null.

questions.question: What does { once: true } do when passed to addEventListener?
options: Invokes the listener at most once, removing it automatically after it fires
Ensures only one listener can ever exist for that event type
Fires the listener once per animation frame
Defers the listener to run after all others
hints: The option affects the listener's lifetime.
No manual removeEventListener needed afterwards.
questions.explanation: With once: true, the listener is invoked at most once after being added and is automatically removed when invoked. No manual removeEventListener required.

questions.question: Which selector styles a <section> only when it contains an element with class featured?
options: section:has(.featured)
section .featured
section > .featured
section:contains(.featured)
hints: You are selecting the parent, not the descendant.
One modern pseudo-class takes relative selectors as its argument.
questions.explanation: :has() represents an element if any of the relative selectors passed as its argument match when anchored against it — providing a way to select a parent (or preceding sibling) based on its contents, which plain descendant selectors cannot do.

questions.question: What is the CSS rem unit relative to?
options: The font-size of the root element
The font-size of the parent element
The element's own font-size
1% of the viewport width
hints: The r stands for root.
em, by contrast, uses the element's own calculated font-size.
questions.explanation: rem represents the font-size of the root element (typically <html>), commonly 16px by browser default but adjustable by user preference. em instead represents the element's own calculated font-size, which is why nested em values compound while rem stays stable.

questions.question: Before descendants of a card can respond to @container size queries, what must be set on the container element?
options: container-type: inline-size (or size)
display: container
overflow: hidden
position: relative
hints: The container must be established as a query container first.
One value queries the inline axis; another queries both dimensions.
questions.explanation: Size-based container queries require establishing a query container: container-type: inline-size establishes one for dimensional queries on the inline axis, and size for both inline and block dimensions. Without it, @container size queries have nothing to measure against.

questions.question: You need to react when one specific element's box changes size — even if the viewport does not change. Which API fits?
options: ResizeObserver
The window resize event
MutationObserver
IntersectionObserver
hints: Window resize only reflects viewport changes.
The right interface reports content- and border-box dimension changes.
questions.explanation: ResizeObserver reports changes to the dimensions of an element's content or border box, responding to element size changes even when they have nothing to do with the viewport — which the window resize event cannot do.

questions.question: Which statement about service workers is true?
options: They run in a worker context on a separate thread and have no DOM access
They can read and modify the DOM directly
They run on the main thread between tasks
They work on any HTTP page
hints: They are designed to be fully asynchronous.
They are also restricted to secure contexts (with a localhost exception).
questions.explanation: Service workers run in a worker context: no DOM access, on a different thread from the main JavaScript, non-blocking and fully asynchronous. They are also limited to secure contexts — HTTPS, with http://localhost treated as secure for development.

questions.question: What does inputmode="numeric" on an input actually do?
options: Hints the browser to show a numeric virtual keyboard, without enforcing any validation
Restricts the field so only digits can be typed
Validates the value as a number on form submission
Converts the submitted value to a Number type
hints: It is a hint about which virtual keyboard to display.
MDN notes it doesn't cause any validity requirements to be enforced.
questions.explanation: inputmode hints at the kind of data expected so browsers can show a fitting virtual keyboard — numeric shows a digits keyboard. It enforces nothing: MDN states the attribute doesn't cause any validity requirements to be enforced on input.

questions.question: You give a <div> role="button" and a click handler. What must you add for keyboard users?
options: Key event handlers that activate it on Enter and Space (and make it focusable)
Nothing — role="button" adds keyboard behavior
Only an Enter key handler; Space is optional
An aria-pressed attribute
hints: role="button" changes semantics, not behavior.
Native <button> elements provide all of this by default.
questions.explanation: First: stop, go back, and do not do this. Good. Now, with role="button" on a non-button element, click handlers fire only for pointer clicks — separate key event handlers must be added so the control activates on Space and Enter (and it must be focusable). Native buttons provide keyboard and focus behavior by default, which is why MDN recommends them.
